dhpak1.10:1.1: 1.9 The Story about the Elder Nanda Nandattheravatthu
dhpak1.10:2.1: “Just as the rain can penetrate,” {1.115} this Dhamma teaching was given by the Teacher while he was in residence at
dhpak1.10:2.2: Jetavana with reference to venerable Nanda.
dhpak1.10:4.1: For after the Teacher had set in motion the glorious Wheel of the Dhamma, he went forth to Rājagaha and took up his residence at Veḷuvana.
dhpak1.10:4.2: Thereupon his father, the great king Suddhodana, sent ten ambassadors to him, one after the other, each with a retinue of
dhpak1.10:4.3: a thousand men, saying to them: “Fetch my son here and show him to me [28.218] before my face.” After nine ambassadors had gone there,
dhpak1.10:4.4: attained Arahatship, and failed to return, Elder Kāḷa Udāyī went there and attained Arahatship. And knowing that it was
dhpak1.10:4.5: the proper time for the Teacher to go, he described the beauties of the journey and conducted the Teacher with his retinue
dhpak1.10:4.6: of twenty thousand Arahats to Kapilapura. And there, in the company of his kinsfolk, the Teacher, taking a shower of rain
dhpak1.10:4.7: for his text, related the Birth Story about Vessantara. On the following day he entered the city for alms.
dhpak1.10:4.8: By the recitation of the verse: “One should strive and not be heedless,” he established his father in the fruition of Stream-entry;
dhpak1.10:4.9: and by the recitation of the verse: “One should live by Dhamma,” he established Mahā Pajāpatī in the fruition of Stream-entry
dhpak1.10:4.10: and his father in the fruition of Once-returning. And at the end of the meal, with reference to the praise bestowed on
dhpak1.10:4.11: him by the mother of Rāhula, he related the Birth Story about the Kinnara Canda.
dhpak1.10:5.1: On the following day, while the ceremonies of Prince Nanda’s consecration, house-warming, and marriage were in progress,
dhpak1.10:5.2: the Teacher entered the house for alms, placed his bowl in Prince Nanda’s hands, and wished him good luck.
dhpak1.10:5.3: Then, rising from his seat, he departed without taking his bowl from the hands of the prince. Out of reverence for the Realised One,
dhpak1.10:5.4: Prince Nanda did not dare say: “Venerable Sir, receive your bowl,” but thought within himself: “He will take his bowl at
dhpak1.10:5.5: the head of the stairs.” But even when the Teacher reached the head of the stairs, he did not take his bowl. Thought Nanda:
dhpak1.10:5.6: “He will take his bowl at the foot of the stairs.” But the Teacher did not take his bowl even there. {1.116} Thought Nanda:
dhpak1.10:5.7: “He will take his bowl in the palace court.” But the Teacher did not take his bowl even there. Prince Nanda desired greatly
dhpak1.10:5.8: to return to his bride, and followed the Teacher much against his own will. But so great was his reverence for the Teacher
dhpak1.10:5.9: that he did not dare say: “Receive your bowl,” but continued to follow the Teacher, thinking to himself: “He will take his bowl here!
dhpak1.10:5.10: He will take his bowl there!”
dhpak1.10:6.1: At that moment they brought word to his bride Janapada Kaḷyāṇī: “My lady, the Fortunate One has taken Prince Nanda away with him;
dhpak1.10:6.2: it is his purpose to deprive you of him.” Thereupon Janapada Kaḷyāṇī, with tears streaming down her face and hair half-combed,
dhpak1.10:6.3: ran after Prince Nanda as fast as she could [28.219] and said to him: “Noble sir, please return quickly.”
dhpak1.10:6.4: Her words caused a quiver in Nanda’s heart; but the Teacher, without so much as taking his bowl, led him to the monastery and said to him:
dhpak1.10:6.5: “Nanda, would you like to go forth?” So great was Prince Nanda’s reverence for the Buddha that he refrained from saying:
dhpak1.10:6.6: “I do not wish to go forth,” and said instead: “Yes, I should like to go forth.” The Teacher said: “Well then, let Nanda go forth.”
dhpak1.10:6.7: Thus it happened that on the third day after the Teacher’s arrival at Kapilapura he caused Nanda to go forth.
dhpak1.10:7.1: On the seventh day the mother of Rāhula adorned Prince Rāhula and sent him to the Fortunate One, saying: “Dear son,
dhpak1.10:7.2: go look upon this ascetic, possessed of a retinue of twenty thousand ascetics, possessed of a body of the hue of gold,
dhpak1.10:7.3: possessed of the beauty of form of Mahā Brahma. This ascetic is your father. To him once belonged great stores of treasure.
dhpak1.10:7.4: From the time of his Great Renunciation we have not seen him. Ask him for this your inheritance, saying: ‘Dear father,
dhpak1.10:7.5: I am a royal prince, and so soon as I shall receive the ceremonial consecration, I shall become a Universal Monarch.
dhpak1.10:7.6: I have need of wealth; bestow wealth upon me; for to a son belongs the wealth which formerly belonged to his father.’”
dhpak1.10:8.1: Accordingly Prince Rāhula went to the Fortunate One. The moment he saw him he conceived a warm affection for his father,
dhpak1.10:8.2: and his heart rejoiced within him. And he said: “Ascetic, pleasant is your shadow,” {1.117} and said much else befitting his own station.
dhpak1.10:8.3: When the Fortunate One had finished his meal, he pronounced the words of thanksgiving, arose from his seat, and departed.
dhpak1.10:9.1: Prince Rāhula followed in the footsteps of the Fortunate One, saying: “Ascetic, give me my inheritance; ascetic,
dhpak1.10:9.2: give me my inheritance.” The Fortunate One did not repel the prince; even the attendants were unable to prevent the prince
dhpak1.10:9.3: from accompanying the Fortunate One. In this manner the prince accompanied the Fortunate One to the grove.
dhpak1.10:9.4: Then the thought occurred to the Fortunate One: “The paternal inheritance which this youth seeks inevitably brings destruction in its train.
dhpak1.10:9.5: Behold, I will bestow upon him the sevenfold noble inheritance which I received at the foot of the Bodhi tree;
dhpak1.10:9.6: I will make him master of an inheritance which transcends the world.”
dhpak1.10:10.1: Therefore the Fortunate One addressed Venerable Sāriputta: “Well then, Sāriputta, let Prince Rāhula go forth.”
dhpak1.10:10.2: When, however, Prince Rāhula had gone forth, the king his grandfather was afflicted with great sorrow. Unable to endure his sorrow,
dhpak1.10:10.3: [28.220] he made known his sorrow to the Fortunate One and made the following request of him: “It were well, venerable Sir,
dhpak1.10:10.4: if the noble bhikkhus did not give the going forth to any youth without the permission of his mother and father.”
dhpak1.10:10.5: The Fortunate One granted him this request.
dhpak1.10:11.1: Again one day, as the Fortunate One sat in the royal palace after breakfast, the king, sitting respectfully at one side,
dhpak1.10:11.2: said to the Fortunate One: “Venerable Sir, while you were practicing your austerities, a certain Deva approached me and said to me:
dhpak1.10:11.3: ‘Your son is dead.’ But I refused to believe him and replied: ‘My son will not die until he attains Awakening.’”
dhpak1.10:11.4: The Fortunate One said: “Now will you believe? In a previous existence also, when a Deva showed you bones and said to you:
dhpak1.10:11.5: ‘Your son is dead,’ you refused to believe it.” And with reference to this incident he related the The Long Birth Story about Dhammapāla.
dhpak1.10:11.6: At the conclusion of the story the king was established in the fruition of Non-returning.
dhpak1.10:13.1: When the Fortunate One had thus established his father in the three fruitions, {1.118} he returned once more to Rājagaha,
dhpak1.10:13.2: accompanied by the assembly of bhikkhus. Now he had promised Anāthapiṇḍika to visit Sāvatthī, so soon as the great monastery
dhpak1.10:13.3: of Jetavana should be completed, and receiving word shortly afterwards that the monastery had been completed,
dhpak1.10:13.4: he went to Jetavana and took up his residence there. While the Teacher was thus residing at Jetavana, venerable Nanda,
dhpak1.10:13.5: becoming discontented, told his troubles to the bhikkhus, saying: “Friends, I am dissatisfied. I am now living the spiritual life,
dhpak1.10:13.6: but I cannot endure to live the spiritual life any longer. I intend to abandon the higher precepts and to return to the lower life,
dhpak1.10:13.7: the life of a lay disciple.”
dhpak1.10:14.1: The Fortunate One, hearing of this incident, sent for Venerable Nanda and said this to him: “Nanda, is the report true
dhpak1.10:14.2: that you spoke as follows to a large company of bhikkhus: ‘Friends, I am dissatisfied; I am now living the spiritual life,
dhpak1.10:14.3: but I cannot endure to live the spiritual life any longer; I intend to abandon the higher precepts and to return to the lower life,
dhpak1.10:14.4: the life of a lay disciple’?” – “It is quite true, venerable Sir.” – “But, Nanda, why are you dissatisfied with the
dhpak1.10:14.5: spiritual life you are now living? Why can you not endure to live the spiritual life any longer? Why do you intend to
dhpak1.10:14.6: abandon the higher precepts and [28.221] to return to the lower life, the life of a lay disciple?” – “Venerable Sir,
dhpak1.10:14.7: when I left my house, my noble wife Janapada Kaḷyāṇī, with hair half-combed, took leave of me, saying: ‘Noble sir,
dhpak1.10:14.8: please return immediately.’ Venerable Sir, it is because I keep remembering her that I am dissatisfied with the religious
dhpak1.10:14.9: life I am now living; that I cannot endure to live the spiritual life any longer; that I intend to abandon the higher
dhpak1.10:14.10: precepts and to return to the lower life, the life of a lay disciple.”
dhpak1.10:15.1: Ordained in Body Then the Fortunate One took venerable Nanda by the arm, and by psychic power conducted him to the Realm
dhpak1.10:15.2: of the Thirty-Three. On the way the Fortunate One pointed out to venerable Nanda in a certain burnt field, seated on a burnt stump,
dhpak1.10:15.3: a greedy monkey which had lost her ears and nose and tail in a fire.
dhpak1.10:16.1: When they reached the Realm of the Thirty-Three, he pointed out five hundred pink-footed Accharās who came to wait upon Sakka,
dhpak1.10:16.2: the Lord of the Devas. {1.119} And when the Fortunate One had shown venerable Nanda these two sights, he asked him this question:
dhpak1.10:16.3: “Nanda, which do you regard as being the more beautiful and fair to look upon and handsome, your noble wife Janapada
dhpak1.10:16.4: Kaḷyāṇī or these five hundred pink-footed Accharās?”
dhpak1.10:17.1: “Venerable Sir,” replied Nanda, “as far inferior as this greedy monkey which has lost her ears and nose and tail is to
dhpak1.10:17.2: Janapada Kaḷyāṇī, even so far inferior, venerable Sir, is my noble wife Janapada Kaḷyāṇī to these five hundred pink-footed Accharās.
dhpak1.10:17.3: In comparison with these Accharās my noble wife does not come into the count; she does not come within a fraction of them,
dhpak1.10:17.4: she does not come within a fraction of a fraction of them; on the contrary, these five hundred pink-footed Accharās are
dhpak1.10:17.5: infinitely more beautiful and fair to look upon and handsome.”
dhpak1.10:18.1: “Cheer up, Nanda!” replied the Fortunate One. “I guarantee that you will win these five hundred pink-footed Accharās.”
dhpak1.10:18.2: Venerable Nanda said: “If, venerable Sir, the Fortunate One guarantees that I shall win these five hundred pink-footed Accharās,
dhpak1.10:18.3: in that case, venerable Sir, I shall take the greatest pleasure in living the exalted life of a monastic.”
dhpak1.10:19.1: Then the Fortunate One, taking venerable Nanda with him, disappeared from the Realm of the Thirty-Three and reappeared at Jetavana.
dhpak1.10:19.2: Now it was not long before the bhikkhus heard the following report: “It appears that it is in the hope of winning Accharās
dhpak1.10:19.3: that venerable Nanda, brother of the Fortunate One, son of his mother’s sister, is living the religious life;
dhpak1.10:19.4: it appears that [28.222] the Fortunate One has guaranteed that he shall win five hundred pink-footed Accharās.”
dhpak1.10:20.1: As a result venerable Nanda’s fellow bhikkhus treated him as a hireling and as one bought with a price.
dhpak1.10:20.2: And they addressed him accordingly, saying: “It appears that venerable Nanda is a hireling; it appears that venerable
dhpak1.10:20.3: Nanda is one bought with a price. It appears that it is in the hope of winning Accharās that he is living the religious life;
dhpak1.10:20.4: it appears that the Fortunate One has guaranteed that he shall win five hundred pink-footed Accharās.”
dhpak1.10:21.1: Now venerable Nanda, {1.120} although his fellow bhikkhus despised him, were ashamed of him, and tormented him by calling
dhpak1.10:21.2: him “hireling” and “a bought man,” nevertheless, living in solitude, withdrawn from the world, heedful, ardent, resolute,
dhpak1.10:21.3: in no long time, even in this life, himself abode in the knowledge, realisation, and attainment of that supreme goal of
dhpak1.10:21.4: the spiritual life for the sake of which youth of good families go forth from the household life to the houseless life.
dhpak1.10:21.5: This did he know: “Destroyed is rebirth, accomplished is the spiritual life, done is what ought to be done,
dhpak1.10:21.6: there is no more of this mundane state, this he knew.” And there was yet another venerable elder numbered among the Arahats.
dhpak1.10:22.1: Now a certain Devatā came by night to the Teacher, illuminating the whole Jetavana; and bowing to the Teacher, thus addressed him:
dhpak1.10:22.2: “Venerable Sir, venerable Nanda, son of the sister of the mother of the Fortunate One, by extinction of the pollutants,
dhpak1.10:22.3: even in this life, himself abides in the knowledge, realisation, and attainment of freedom from the pollutants,
dhpak1.10:22.4: emancipation of the heart, emancipation of the intellect. And there arose within the Fortunate One also knowledge of the following:
dhpak1.10:22.5: “Through the destruction of the pollutants, Nanda, without pollutants, freed in mind, freed through wisdom, dwells having known,
dhpak1.10:22.6: having directly experienced, and having attained (Nibbāna) himself in this very life.”
dhpak1.10:23.1: In the course of the same night venerable Nanda also approached the Fortunate One, bowed to him, and spoke as follows:
dhpak1.10:23.2: “Venerable Sir, I release the Fortunate One from the promise which he made when he, the Fortunate One, guaranteed that I
dhpak1.10:23.3: should win five hundred pink-footed Accharās.” The Fortunate One replied: “Nanda, I myself grasped your mind with my own mind and saw:
dhpak1.10:23.4: ‘Through the destruction of the pollutants, Nanda, {1.121} without pollutants, freed in mind, freed through wisdom,
dhpak1.10:23.5: dwells having known, having directly experienced, and having attained (Nibbāna) himself in this very life.’
dhpak1.10:23.6: Likewise a Devatā informed me of the fact, saying: ‘Through the destruction [28.223] of the pollutants, Nanda,
dhpak1.10:23.7: without pollutants, freed in mind, freed through wisdom, dwells having known, having directly experienced,
dhpak1.10:23.8: and having attained (Nibbāna) himself in this very life.’ When, therefore, Nanda, you ceased to cling to the things of the world,
dhpak1.10:23.9: and your heart was released from the pollutants, at that moment I was released from that promise.” Then the Fortunate One,
dhpak1.10:23.10: understanding the matter, uttered the following exalted utterance:
dhpak1.10:24.1: He who has got out of the mud, who crushed the thorn of sense desire, who arrived at delusion’s destruction, in pleasure and pain that monk does not shake.
dhpak1.10:25.1: Now one day the bhikkhus approached venerable Nanda and asked him: “Friend Nanda, aforetime you said: ‘I am dissatisfied.’
dhpak1.10:25.2: Do you say the same thing now?” – “Friends, I am in no wise inclined to the life of a lay disciple.”
dhpak1.10:25.3: When the bhikkhus heard his answer, they said: “Venerable Nanda says that which is not true, utters falsehood.
dhpak1.10:25.4: In former days he used to say: ‘I am dissatisfied,’ but now says: ‘I am in no wise inclined to the life of a lay disciple.”
dhpak1.10:25.5: And forthwith they went and reported the matter to the Fortunate One.
dhpak1.10:26.1: The Fortunate One replied: “Bhikkhus, in former days Nanda’s personality was like an ill-thatched house, but now it has
dhpak1.10:26.2: come to be like a well-thatched house. From the day he saw the divine Accharās, he has striven to reach the goal of the
dhpak1.10:26.3: duties of one gone forth, {1.122} and now he has done his duty.” So saying, he pronounced the following verses:
dhpak1.10:27.1: 13. Yathā agāraṁ ducchannaṁ vuṭṭhī samativijjhati, evaṁ abhāvitaṁ cittaṁ rāgo samativijjhati.
dhpak1.10:28.1: Just as the rain can penetrate a house with thatching that is poor, so also passion penetrates a mind that is undeveloped.
dhpak1.10:29.1: 14. Yathā agāraṁ succhannaṁ vuṭṭhī na samativijjhati, evaṁ subhāvitaṁ cittaṁ rāgo na samativijjhati.
dhpak1.10:30.1: Just as rain does not penetrate a house with thatching that is good, so passion cannot penetrate a mind that is well-developed.
dhpak1.10:31.1: At the conclusion of the verses many reached the fruition of Stream-entry, and many people had benefit from the teaching.
dhpak1.10:32.1: Well Thatched House The bhikkhus began to discuss the incident in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, the Buddhas are marvelous!
dhpak1.10:32.2: Venerable Nanda became dissatisfied with the spiritual life all because of Janapada Kaḷyāṇī; but the Teacher,
dhpak1.10:32.3: employing Devaccharās as a lure, won him to complete obedience.”
dhpak1.10:33.1: The Teacher came in and asked them: “Bhikkhus, what is it you are sitting here now talking about?” When they told him, he said:
dhpak1.10:33.2: “Bhikkhus, {1.123} this is not the first time Nanda has been won to obedience by the lure of the opposite sex;
dhpak1.10:33.3: the same thing happened in a previous existence also.” So saying, he related the following [28.224]
dhpak1.10:34.1: 9c Story of the Past: Kappaṭa and the Donkey
dhpak1.10:35.1: Once upon a time, when Brahmadatta reigned in Bārāṇasī, there dwelt at Bārāṇasī a merchant named Kappaṭa.
dhpak1.10:35.2: Now Kappaṭa had a donkey which used to carry loads of pottery for him, and every day he used to go a journey of seven leagues.
dhpak1.10:35.3: On a certain occasion Kappaṭa loaded his donkey down with a load of pottery and took him to Takkasilā.
dhpak1.10:36.1: While he was engaged in disposing of his wares, he allowed the donkey to run loose. As the donkey wandered along the bank of a ditch,
dhpak1.10:36.2: he saw a female of his own species and straightaway went up to her. She gave him a friendly greeting and said to him:
dhpak1.10:36.3: “Where have you come from?” – “From Bārāṇasī.” – “On what errand?” – “On business.” – “How big a load do you carry?”
dhpak1.10:36.4: – “A big load of pottery.” – “How many leagues do you travel, carrying a big load like that?” – “Seven leagues.”
dhpak1.10:36.5: – “In the various places you visit, is there anyone to rub your feet and your back?” – “No.” – “If that’s the case,
dhpak1.10:36.6: you must have a mighty hard time.”
dhpak1.10:37.1: Of course animals have no one to rub their feet and their back; she said this merely to join bonds of love between them.
dhpak1.10:38.1: As the result of her talk, the donkey became dissatisfied. After the merchant had disposed of his wares, he returned to
dhpak1.10:38.2: the donkey and said to him: “Come, let’s be off.” – “Go yourself; I won’t go.” {1.124} Over and over again the merchant
dhpak1.10:38.3: tried with gentle words to persuade him to go; and when, in spite of his efforts, the donkey remained balky, he vented abuse upon him.
dhpak1.10:38.4: Finally he thought to himself: “I know a way to make him go,” and pronounced the following verse:
dhpak1.10:39.1: I make a goad for you, with a sixteen-inch thorn, I will cut your body, you should know this, donkey.
dhpak1.10:40.1: When the donkey heard that, he said: “In that case I shall know just what to do to you.” So saying, he pronounced the following verse:
dhpak1.10:41.1: You make a goad for me, with a sixteen-inch thorn, I will plant my fore feet, and kick with my back feet, and knock your
dhpak1.10:41.2: teeth right out, you should know, Kappaṭa!
dhpak1.10:42.1: When the merchant heard that, he thought to himself: “What can be the reason for his talking thus?”
dhpak1.10:42.2: The merchant looked this way and that, and finally his eyes fell upon the female donkey. “Ah!” thought the merchant to himself,
dhpak1.10:42.3: “she must have taught him these tricks. I will [28.225] say to the donkey: ‘I will bring you home a mate like that.’
dhpak1.10:42.4: Thus, by employing the lure of the opposite sex, I will make him go.” Accordingly he pronounced the following verse:
dhpak1.10:43.1: A four-footed female, with a pearly face, having every mark of beauty, a wife will I bring to you, you should know this, donkey.
dhpak1.10:44.1: When the donkey heard that, his heart rejoiced, and he replied with the following verse:
dhpak1.10:45.1: A four-footed female, with a pearly face, having every mark of beauty, a wife you will bring to me, you should know,
dhpak1.10:45.2: Kappaṭa, Kappaṭa, I will go further, (I will go) fourteen leagues a day!
dhpak1.10:46.1: “Well then,” said Kappaṭa, “come!” And taking the donkey with him, he went back to the place where he had left the cart.
dhpak1.10:47.1: After a few days the donkey said to him: “Didn’t you say to me: ‘I will bring you a mate’?” The merchant replied:
dhpak1.10:47.2: “Yes, I said just that, and I will not break my word; I will bring you home a mate. But I will provide food only for you.
dhpak1.10:47.3: It may or may not be enough for both you and your mate, but that is a matter for you alone to decide.
dhpak1.10:47.4: After you both have lived together, foals will be born to you. The food I shall give you may or may not be enough for both
dhpak1.10:47.5: you and your mate and your foals too, but that is a matter for you alone to decide.” As the merchant spoke these words,
dhpak1.10:48.1: When the Teacher had ended his lesson, he concluded the Birth Story as follows: “At that time, bhikkhus,
dhpak1.10:48.2: the female donkey was Janapada Kaḷyāṇī, the male donkey was Nanda, and the merchant was I myself. In former times, too,
dhpak1.10:48.3: Nanda was won to obedience by the lure of the female sex.”
